before: Git has separate places for your working edits and the next commit’s staged snapshot. Inspecting one does not automatically inspect the other.
Imagine note.txt was committed as Moon. You edit it to Sea and stage it, then edit it again to Sky without staging. The staged snapshot still says Sea.

```bash
git diff -- note.txt
git diff --cached -- note.txt
```

git diff compares working files with the index, so the first command shows Sea becoming Sky. --cached compares the index with HEAD, so the second shows Moon becoming Sea. -- separates options from the named path. These commands inspect changes; they do not stage or commit them.
Changed situation: After the scenario above, what content would a commit of the current index record?
The index contains Sea. The later Sky edit is still only in the working tree.
after: Working files hold your current edits. The index holds the version staged for the next commit. These can differ.
Suppose note.txt was committed as Moon. You change it to Sea and run git add note.txt. Then you change it to Sky without staging again. The index still contains Sea.

These commands inspect the two differences.

```bash
git diff -- note.txt
git diff --cached -- note.txt
```
git diff shows the change from staged Sea to working Sky. git diff --cached shows the change from committed Moon to staged Sea. -- separates command options from the file path.
A normal git commit records the index. In this situation it saves Sea, while Sky remains an unstaged change.
Neither diff command stages or commits anything. Use both when you need to inspect what is saved for the next commit and what is still outside it.
